intro.heading: Treatment Library
intro.sub: Your one-stop-shop for therapy resources — vetted clinical assessment tools, community referrals, and youth and family handouts, all searchable in one place and selected to help reduce youth suicidal ideation.
intro.pdfNotice: PDF files for each resource are being finalized and will appear here as they're added. Items below show what each resource is and why it's included, even before its file is uploaded.

items.title: Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS)
items.description: A structured interview used to assess the severity and immediacy of suicidal ideation and behavior. Used at intake and re-administered as risk status changes throughout treatment.
items.evidence: A widely adopted, extensively studied risk-assessment instrument used across clinical and research settings for suicide risk stratification.

items.title: Stanley-Brown Safety Planning Intervention
items.description: A brief, collaborative worksheet completed with the client (and caregivers, when appropriate) that identifies warning signs, coping strategies, support contacts, and steps to reduce access to lethal means.
items.evidence: One of the most widely studied and disseminated safety-planning approaches in suicide prevention care.

items.title: DBT Skills: Distress Tolerance & Emotion Regulation
items.description: Skill-building handouts adapted from Dialectical Behavior Therapy to help clients tolerate intense emotions and reduce crisis-driven behavior.
items.evidence: DBT has a substantial evidence base for reducing self-harm and suicidal behavior, including in adolescent populations.

items.title: CBT Cognitive Restructuring Techniques
items.description: Guided worksheets to help clients identify, examine, and reframe unhelpful thought patterns that contribute to distress.
items.evidence: CBT is one of the most extensively researched therapeutic approaches for youth depression and anxiety.

items.title: Behavioral Activation Planning Sheet
items.description: Helps clients schedule small, achievable, values-aligned activities to counter withdrawal and low mood.
items.evidence: Behavioral activation is a well-established, evidence-based component of depression treatment.

items.title: Vetted Mental Health Referrals
items.description: A curated, regularly updated list of community mental health providers for step-down or ongoing care once Rise treatment ends.
items.evidence: Maintained and vetted directly by the Rise and CU Boulder team based on client feedback and provider responsiveness.

items.title: Post-Rise Therapy Options
items.description: A guide to what happens after the Rise treatment window ends, including options by insurance status and geography.
items.evidence: Compiled from partner agency intake criteria and updated as availability changes.

items.title: How to Support Your Teen: A Family Guide
items.description: Plain-language psychoeducation for caregivers on what to expect during treatment and how to support a teen at home.
items.evidence: Grounded in family-inclusive treatment literature; detailed citations to be added.

items.title: Family Engagement Guide
items.description: Suggestions for clinicians on involving caregivers productively in treatment, even in higher-conflict households.
items.evidence: Grounded in family-inclusive treatment literature; detailed citations to be added.

items.title: Youth Coping Skills Worksheet
items.description: A self-guided worksheet helping youth identify and practice personal coping strategies for distress.
items.evidence: Grounded in CBT/DBT coping-skills literature; detailed citations to be added.

items.title: Youth Safety Planning Template
items.description: A youth-facing version of the safety plan, written in accessible language for the client to keep and reference.
items.evidence: Adapted from the Stanley-Brown Safety Planning Intervention for a youth reading level.

items.title: Mindfulness & Grounding Tools
items.description: Brief grounding exercises youth can use independently between sessions to manage acute distress.
items.evidence: Grounded in mindfulness-based intervention literature; detailed citations to be added.

items.title: School Navigation Tip Sheet
items.description: Practical guidance for navigating school partnership complexities, coordinating with counselors, and managing referrals.
items.evidence: Compiled from therapist co-design sessions on real school-coordination challenges.

items.title: District-Specific Info Guides
items.description: Detailed guides for the schools and districts Rise frequently partners with, including key contacts and procedures.
items.evidence: Compiled and maintained directly by the Rise team.

items.title: Multi-System Coordination Guide
items.description: Resources for collaborating across hospitals, clinics, and school teams when a case spans multiple systems.
items.evidence: Compiled from therapist co-design sessions on real multi-system cases.

items.title: Psychoeducation
items.description: Teaching the youth or caregiver about the nature of a youth’s problem, contributing factors to a problem, and/or rationale and description of a proposed intervention.

links.label: Teen Depression: More Than Just Moodiness (NIMH)
Suicidal feelings: guide for young people (YoungMinds)

items.title: Therapeutic Alliance/Relationship Building
items.description: Developing a trusting, supportive and engaging relationship between clinical providers and patients.

items.title: Addressing Treatment Barriers
items.description: Therapist identifies, inquires about, or aims to reduce barriers to treatment participation. This may include problem solving about practical barriers to attendance, or discussing or improving the feasibility of assigned homework action.

items.title: Commitment to Safety
items.description: Obtaining a commitment from youth to follow safety plan. Note that this is NOT a no suicide contract. Evidence does not support use of no suicide contracts, but many evidence-based treatments integrate youth commitment to utilizing safety plan when experiencing suicidal and/or self-harm urges.

items.title: Safety Planning
items.description: Engaging in safety planning exercises where specific methods of coping during an acute suicidal or self-harm crisis are identified.

links.label: Safety plan template (American Academy of Pediatrics)
Safety Planning Guide: Quick Guide for Clinicians (Suicide Prevention Resource Center)
Make A Safety Plan (in this toolkit)

items.title: Means Safety/Lethal Means Restriction
items.description: Lethal means counseling is assessing whether a person at risk for suicide has access to a firearm or other lethal means, and working with them and their family and support system to limit their access until they are no longer at elevated risk.

items.title: Distress Tolerance
items.description: Skills that assist youth in navigating an emotional crisis and staying safe in the moment.

links.label: Open-source list of DBT distress tolerance skills and descriptions

items.title: Emotion Regulation
items.description: Skills to help youth with naming and understanding their own emotions, decrease the frequency of unpleasant emotions, decrease vulnerability to emotions, and decrease emotional suffering. DBT emotion regulation skills include: STOP skill, Opposite Action, ABC PLEASE, Build Mastery, Cope Ahead and Positive Self-Talk.

items.title: Impulse Control
items.description: Skills designed to assist youth in resisting urges to engage in self-harm or other impulsive and/or dangerous behavior.

links.label: Bringing up self-injury with your clients
Research article (Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry)

items.title: Mindfulness
items.description: Mindfulness is an approach where patients learn mindfulness skills to foster acceptance of thoughts and feelings, focusing on present-moment awareness in a nonjudgmental way.

items.title: Problem Solving
items.description: Teaching specific steps to approach and solve future problems for clients.

items.title: Interpersonal Effectiveness Skills
items.description: Interpersonal effectiveness skills are all about improving interactions and relationships with other people. These skills include strategies for getting people to meet your needs, getting them to do what you want, and getting them to take your opinions seriously. The goals are to strengthen existing relationships, build new ones, and end ones that are unhealthy or toxic. These skills include DEAR MAN, GIVE, FAST and Boundary Building.

items.title: Assertiveness Training
items.description: Teaching assertiveness skills with others, which may involve rehearsal of assertive interactions. This may include how to appropriately state wants or needs, how to say “no” to undesired activities, and how to respond when told “no” after stating a request.

items.title: Behavioral Activation/Activity Scheduling
items.description: Identifying enjoyable activities (e.g., helping others, social activities, sports) and making a plan to participate in these activities outside of session to improve mood.

items.title: Cognitive Restructuring
items.description: Skills for practicing a balanced/helpful way of thinking about stressors and the implications of these events.

items.title: Exposure
items.description: Exposure therapy is essentially as it sounds: gradual and repeated exposure to feared situations. Exposures can take many forms. They can be imaginal (imagined feared outcomes or circumstances), or in vivo (take place in real life); they can occur gradually (graduated), or they can take place very quickly and intensely (flooding). Exposures can target situations (situational exposures) or uncomfortable or distressing physical sensations (interoceptive or sensational exposures). Exposure is by far the most successful treatment for anxiety disorders that has been developed to date.

items.title: Trauma Narrative
items.description: Assisting the youth in describing a trauma or really bad experience in detail and repeatedly reviewing this material with the youth. This can include using play to help the child and parent co-create a narrative of the traumatic experience.

links.label: Analogies to introduce the trauma narrative
Dealing With Trauma: A TF-CBT Workbook for Teens

items.title: Live Caregiver-Youth Coaching
items.description: Providing specific and direct guidance to caregivers to use skills during an in-vivo youth-caregiver interaction in session.

items.title: Parent-Child Quality Time
items.description: Increasing youth and caregiver positive/quality one-on-one time.

links.label: Center for Play Therapy therapist and parent resources (in the context of Child-Parent Relationship Therapy)

items.title: Caregiver Coping
items.description: Facilitating caregiver learning or practicing strategies to more effectively handle stressful situations (e.g., self-care, problem-solving about respite, coping skills).

links.label: Strengthening Your Resilience: Take Care of Yourself as You Care for Others
For parents: the importance of self-care
Taking care of yourself and your family

items.title: Youth Education/Academic Support
items.description: Assisting youth with specific academic problems, such as homework or study skills. This may include topics such as organization, time management, problem solving, and positive study skills.

items.title: Progressive Muscle Relaxation
items.description: Actively contracting muscles to create tension and progressively releasing for short-term stress relief.

links.label: Progressive Muscle Relaxation Scripts for Children
VA Resource for Progressive Muscle Relaxation

items.title: Affect Identification/Feeling Thermometer
items.description: Facilitating learning about emotions, including linking emotions with their names, identifying physical sensations associated with emotions, or recognizing environmental cues for particular emotions.

items.title: Cognitive Defusion
items.description: The process of altering the influence of thoughts on behavior by changing one’s relationship to them, rather than attempting to change their content, frequency, or form.

items.title: Worry Time
items.description: Worry time is a scheduled daily period set aside for worrying, used to contain habitual worry and keep it from taking over the rest of the day.
